Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The paper describes IC2D as a drawing tool specifically designed to let blind and visually impaired users create and manipulate graphics, focusing on solving utilitarian accessibility problems (cursor relocation, non-visual feedback, grid-based spatial reference). There is no indication it was derived from an entertainment game or co-designed in a fun-first workshop; it appears as a purpose-built assistive drawing system where the primary utilitarian mechanics (grid, labeling, navigation) were central. This aligns best with a mostly utility-first design.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) unstructured play (i.e., no rules, making art),
        (2) semi-structured play (i.e., playground activities),
        (3) flexible structure with rules (i.e., improv),
        (4) flexible game (i.e., board game with house rules),
        (5) game with rigid rules (i.e., video game)
reasoning: Participants followed specific drawing tasks with clear rules and goals (e.g., draw shapes in specified grid cells, connect specific vertices) within a structured grid-based interface, but they could choose positions/angles and explore images, indicating a flexible but rule-governed activity best matching a flexible structure with rules (3).

        (1) entirely skill-based (i.e., trivia, sports),
        (2) mostly skill-based (i.e., mario kart),
        (3) equally skill and chance-based (i.e., catan),
        (4) mostly chance-based (i.e., Uno),
        (5) entirely chance-based (i.e., all dice)
reasoning: The study tasks involve drawing specific shapes and objects accurately using an interface (e.g., precise placement of circles, triangles, rectangles, and perspective-accurate cubes). Outcomes depend on participants’ drawing and spatial skills, with no random or chance elements described, so the design is entirely skill-based.

        (2) mostly solo (i.e., playing against AI in single-player StarCraft),

        (4) mostly social, but aspects are independent (i.e., house on hill haunt transition),

reasoning: All tasks involve individual participants using the IC2D drawing tool alone to complete drawing and visualization tasks; there is no mention of multiplayer, social interaction, or other players, so the design is entirely solo.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely turn-based (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) follows a set of steps (i.e., viticulture's dynamic turn ordering),
        (3) turns are taken, but some actions can be taken at any time (i.e., pandemic),
        (4) most actions can be taken at any time, but there are some phases (i.e., PvP death reset timer),
        (5) entirely simultaneous (i.e., race)
reasoning: The study is about a single-user drawing interface (IC2D), where users follow ordered steps and keypress sequences to select cells, shapes, and then finalize drawings. There is no notion of multiple players or simultaneous actions; interaction is procedural and stepwise, fitting best with a design that follows a set of steps rather than turn-based or simultaneous play.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely synchronous (i.e., real time strategy game),
        (2) mostly synchronous with a few asynchronous affordances (i.e., league of legends),
        (3) equal mix of synchronous and asynchronous affordances (i.e., helldivers 2),
        (4) mostly asynchronous with few synchronous affordances (i.e. cookie clicker),
        (5) entirely asynchronous (i.e., chess by postage mail)
reasoning: Participants used a single-user drawing program (IC2D) individually, with no mention of real-time or turn-based interaction between multiple users. Tasks involved solo creation and later offline judging, which aligns with an entirely asynchronous interaction structure rather than synchronous multiplayer or mixed-time coordination.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely competitive (i.e., spit card game),
        (2) mostly competitive, but sometimes collaboration is important (i.e., forbidden island),
        (3) mix of competitive and collaborative (i.e., mario party 2 vs 2 mini-games),
        (4) mostly collaborative (i.e., animal crossing),
        (5) entirely collaborative (i.e., pandemic)
reasoning: The study is an HCI evaluation of a drawing tool (IC2D) where individual participants complete drawing tasks; there is no game-like or adversarial interaction between participants. Sighted and visually impaired users are compared by researchers, not put in competition or cooperation with each other. This maps best to an entirely non-competitive, task-focused setting, which aligns most closely with the 'entirely collaborative' category among the given options.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely symmetrical (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) mostly symmetrical (i.e., undertale's differing NPC behaviors based on previous playthroughs),
        (3) both symmetrical and asymmetrical (i.e., pandemic with its similar turn structure but different character abilities),
        (4) mostly asymmetrical (i.e., tag),
        (5) entirely asymmetrical (i.e., keep talking, nobody explodes)
reasoning: All participants, sighted and visually impaired, used the same IC2D grid-based drawing interface, the same tasks, and the same interaction mechanics (keyboard, help mode, labeling). There are no role differences or distinct abilities; conditions differ only by participant characteristics (sighted vs visually impaired, blindfolding), not by game/system role. This corresponds to an entirely symmetrical design.
